---
title: "Making text comparable"
subtitle: "Normalize carefully and keep the display text intact"
description: "Learn how case, spacing, punctuation, and Unicode normalization change workforce text."
categories: [word processing, normalization, workforce research]
---

Related phrases across the 28 text units can differ in formatting.
The flyer heading `RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE` uses capitals, while job details
use ordinary case. Pasted text may also contain extra spacing and accented
characters. The team examines each normalization step's effect before applying
it.

Before counting matches, the team has to decide which small differences to
ignore. Each edit can make comparison easier and also erase information.

**Normalization** applies edits before text comparison.
Common operations change case, trim spaces, remove punctuation, or convert
Unicode characters to a consistent form.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching. The text files are local and fixed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain the purpose of normalization before comparison.
- examine the effects of lowercasing and space repair.
- examine punctuation removal with stringr's ICU regex engine.
- compare two Unicode forms of the same visible word.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Load text with an accent check

The readr package opens CSV files, and dplyr and tibble handle tables.
The stringr package handles text operations, while stringi normalizes Unicode.
The purrr package applies checks to each item.
Inputs contain the Riverton text and feedback with the word `café`.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(stringi)
library(purrr)

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

feedback <- read_csv(
  "data/customer_feedback.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    feedback_id = col_character(),
    submitted_at = col_character(),
    channel = col_character(),
    rating = col_character(),
    comment = col_character()
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(sentences$text[23], "RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE"),
  identical(nrow(feedback), 5L),
  identical(feedback$comment[2], "The café listing was easy to find.")
)
```

The accent check matters because normalization can change text that looks stable
on screen. The visible word may stay the same while the stored code points
change.

## Lowercase text and repair spaces

**Case folding** prepares text for case-insensitive comparison.
This example uses lowercasing, which differs from full Unicode case folding.
The table contains a Riverton string and a copy of `s002` with tripled spaces
to simulate pasted text. It also compares `US` with `us`.

```{r}
padded_requirement <- str_replace_all(
  sentences$text[sentences$sentence_id == "s002"],
  " ",
  "   "
)
padded_requirement <- paste0("  ", padded_requirement, "  ")

case_space_examples <- tibble(
  example = c(
    "Flyer heading",
    "Padded requirement sentence",
    "Warning pair, capital",
    "Warning pair, lower"
  ),
  raw_text = c(
    sentences$text[sentences$sentence_id == "s023"],
    padded_requirement,
    "US",
    "us"
  ),
  lowercased = str_to_lower(raw_text),
  squished = str_squish(raw_text)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| html-table-processing: none

knitr::kable(
  case_space_examples,
  col.names = c("Example", "Raw text", "Lowercased", "Spacing normalized"),
  caption = "Lowercasing and spacing changes",
  format = "html",
  table.attr = 'class="caption-top table table-sm table-striped small" style="white-space: pre-wrap;"',
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(case_space_examples$lowercased[1], "riverton skills open house"),
  identical(case_space_examples$squished[2], "No prior data experience is required."),
  identical(case_space_examples$lowercased[3], case_space_examples$lowercased[4]),
  identical(str_length(case_space_examples$raw_text[2]), 51L)
)
```

Lowercasing makes `RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE` easier to compare with ordinary
case. It also makes `US` and `us` the same string. `str_squish()` removes leading
and trailing spaces and replaces repeated spaces with one space.

## Remove punctuation only when it is safe

Punctuation removal can make matching easier, but it can damage units such as
`12-week`. The next table uses Riverton strings that contain hyphens,
apostrophes, and periods.

```{r}
punctuation_examples <- tibble(
  sentence_id = c("s001", "s015", "s017"),
  raw_text = sentences$text[match(sentence_id, sentences$sentence_id)],
  without_punctuation = str_remove_all(raw_text, "[[:punct:]]")
)

unicode_punctuation_check <- str_remove_all("“paid—training”", "[[:punct:]]")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  punctuation_examples,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Raw text", "After punctuation removal"),
  caption = "Punctuation removal can remove useful distinctions",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    punctuation_examples$without_punctuation[1],
    "Paid 12week training is provided"
  ),
  identical(
    punctuation_examples$without_punctuation[2],
    "Onthejob training is provided"
  ),
  identical(
    punctuation_examples$without_punctuation[3],
    "A valid drivers license is required"
  ),
  identical(unicode_punctuation_check, "paidtraining")
)
```

Punctuation removal deletes the hyphen in `12-week` and the apostrophe in
`driver's`. The function `str_remove_all()` uses stringr's ICU engine.
Its `[[:punct:]]` class covers Unicode punctuation, such as curly quotes and
em dashes from word processors.

## Normalize Unicode forms

Unicode stores text as code points.
In `café`, the letter `é` can occupy one code point or combine `e` with a
separate accent. NFC keeps the composed form.
NFD separates the accent into its own code point.

```{r}
cafe_word <- str_extract(feedback$comment[2], "café")
cafe_nfc <- stri_trans_nfc(cafe_word)
cafe_nfd <- stri_trans_nfd(cafe_word)

unicode_forms <- tibble(
  form = c("NFC", "NFD"),
  text = c(cafe_nfc, cafe_nfd),
  code_point_count = str_length(text),
  bytes_utf8 = nchar(text, type = "bytes"),
  code_points = map_chr(text, \(value) paste(utf8ToInt(value), collapse = ", "))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  unicode_forms,
  col.names = c("Form", "Text", "Code points", "Bytes as UTF-8", "Code point values"),
  caption = "Two Unicode forms of the visible word 'café'",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(cafe_word, "café"),
  identical(cafe_nfc, "café"),
  !identical(cafe_nfc, cafe_nfd),
  identical(unicode_forms$code_point_count, c(4L, 5L)),
  identical(unicode_forms$bytes_utf8, c(5L, 6L)),
  identical(unicode_forms$code_points[2], "99, 97, 102, 101, 769")
)
```

The forms look the same, but `identical()` detects different stored strings.
Both forms show four letters. NFC uses 4 code points and 5 UTF-8 bytes.
NFD uses 5 code points and 6 bytes.
Its accent occupies a separate code point after `e`.

## Keep two columns

Store at least two versions: raw text for display and normalized text for
comparison. Normalize case, spaces, or Unicode form as the task requires.

```{r}
display_and_match <- sentences |>
  filter(sentence_id %in% c("s001", "s023")) |>
  transmute(
    sentence_id,
    display_text = text,
    comparison_text = text |>
      stri_trans_nfc() |>
      str_squish() |>
      str_to_lower()
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  display_and_match,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Display text", "Comparison text"),
  caption = "Keeping display text separate from comparison text",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(display_and_match$display_text[1], "Paid 12-week training is provided."),
  identical(display_and_match$comparison_text[1], "paid 12-week training is provided."),
  identical(display_and_match$comparison_text[2], "riverton skills open house"),
  !identical(display_and_match$display_text[2], display_and_match$comparison_text[2])
)
```

Normalize text for comparison. Keep raw text for display.
Some normalization operations are irreversible.
After lowercasing, `us` does not reveal whether the source was `US` or `us`.
Choose NFC for the comparison column.
This recommended web-text form gives equivalent character sequences a
consistent representation across systems.

## What to remember

- Normalization makes text easier to compare.
- Lowercasing can merge strings that mean different things.
- ICU punctuation classes contain more than keyboard punctuation.
- Unicode forms can look the same while storing different code points.
- Keep the display text and comparison text separate.
- Raw text preserves information that normalization removes.

A normalized column assists matching, not display.
Show readers the original Riverton text that the Lab collected.
